entry: Metropolitan county in the Yorkshire and the Humber region, northern England (pop., 2024: 2,435,236). Covering 2,029 sq km, the county is urbanized at its center. [[Leeds]] lies in the north-east, Wakefield in the south-east, Huddersfield in the south-west and Bradford in the north-west. Created in 1974 from the central West Riding of Yorkshire, it has five metropolitan boroughs (Bradford, Calderdale, Kirklees, Leeds and Wakefield) that work together through the West Yorkshire Combined Authority. Coal, wool and iron ore industries have left a visible legacy in its buildings and architecture.

Westernmost and largest state of Australia (pop., 2024: 2.965 million). Covering 2,527,013 sq km, it ranges from tropical conditions in the Kimberley to desert interior and a [[Mediterranean climate]] in the south-west. About 80 percent of residents live in [[Perth]], the capital. Dirk Hartog's 1616 expedition made the first European landfall, and the Swan River Colony was established in 1829. Granted responsible government in 1890, the colony federated in 1901. Iron ore and gold mining drive the economy.

Western region of Europe, with boundaries that vary by context. The idea of "the West" arose in contrast to "the East" and was first applied to the western half of the ancient Mediterranean world and the Latin West of the Roman Empire. From the [[Renaissance]] and the Age of Discovery, roughly from the 15th century, "the West" gradually replaced "Christendom" as the preferred name for the area. In 1054 the [[East–West Schism]] divided Christianity into Western and Eastern branches, and Protestantism has been a major denomination since the [[Reformation]] in the 16th century. During the [[Cold War]], Europe was divided for 46 years by the [[Iron Curtain]] (1945–1991): the US-led [[NATO]] formed the Western Bloc and the Soviet-led [[Warsaw Pact]] the Eastern Bloc. A 2018 Pew Research Center study found that 71.0 percent of Western Europeans identified as Christians.

Theatre of World War II in Europe. It covered Denmark, Norway, Luxembourg, Belgium, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, France and Germany; the Italian front was a separate theatre. After the "Phoney War" lull, Germany invaded Denmark and Norway in April 1940 and launched the [[Battle of France]] in May. Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Belgium and France capitulated during May and June, and an air war between Germany and Britain climaxed with the [[Battle of Britain]]. The second phase began in June 1944 with the Allied landings in [[Normandy]] and ended with Germany's defeat in May 1945. Germany's last major counteroffensive in the west, the [[Battle of the Bulge]], failed in December 1944–January 1945.

Theatre of World War I in France and Belgium. After Germany invaded Luxembourg and Belgium in August 1914, its advance was halted at the Battle of the Marne, and both sides dug in along trench lines stretching from the North Sea to the Swiss frontier. Offensives from 1915 to 1917 relied on massive artillery bombardments and infantry advances, yet gained little. The [[Battle of Verdun]] (1916) cost a combined 700,000 casualties, the [[Battle of the Somme]] (1916) over a million, and the [[Battle of Passchendaele]] (1917) 487,000. Both sides tried poison gas, aircraft and [[Tank|tanks]]. The German spring offensive of 1918 advanced nearly 100 km (60 miles), the deepest advance since 1914, but it was short-lived. The Allied Hundred Days Offensive caused the German armies to collapse, and the Armistice of 11 November 1918 ended the fighting; the [[Treaty of Versailles]] followed in 1919.

Mountain range along the west coast of India, also called the Sahyadri. Running about 1,600 km (990 mi) from the Tapti River to Kanyakumari district, it traverses Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, [[Karnataka]], [[Kerala]] and [[Tamil Nadu]] along the western edge of the [[Deccan Plateau]]. Formed during the break-up of [[Gondwana]], the range arose when India separated from Africa in the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous periods. Anamudi, at 2,695 m (8,842 ft), is the highest peak. The range intercepts the southwest [[Monsoon|monsoon]] winds, producing rainfall on the western coast, and its rivers drain almost 40% of India's land area. It is a biodiversity hotspot with at least 325 globally threatened species, and it became a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 2012.

Western half of the island of New Guinea, administered by [[Indonesia]] (pop., 2020: 5,437,775). Also called Papua, it was annexed into the [[Dutch East Indies]] when the Dutch Empire, dominant in the spice trade, took its western part. The Dutch remained until 1962, when the territory passed to a United Nations Temporary Executive Authority (UNTEA) and then to Indonesia after the controversial Act of Free Choice in 1969. The interior is predominantly populated by ethnic Papuans, including the Dani of the Baliem Valley, and much of the region is rainforest. Estimates of local languages range from 200 to over 700. The predominant religion is [[Christianity]], followed by [[Islam]], and the main industries are agriculture, fishing, oil production and mining. The largest city is Jayapura.

Western half of the [[Roman Empire]] (395–476), administered separately under its own imperial court. In 286, [[Diocletian]] institutionalized the division by creating the Tetrarchy, with two senior emperors titled Augustus, one in the East and one in the West. On the death of [[Theodosius I]] in 395, the empire passed to his infant sons, Honorius in the West and Arcadius in the East. In 476 the Roman army in the West was defeated at Ravenna by the Germanic leader Odoacer, who deposed Romulus Augustulus; the event was popularized as the fall of the Western Roman Empire by [[Edward Gibbon]]. The Western imperial court in [[Ravenna]] disappeared by 554, at the end of Justinian's Gothic War. [[Justinian I]] had briefly re-imposed direct rule on North Africa, Italy and parts of Hispania, but these territories were gradually lost. Charlemagne's papal coronation as emperor in 800 revived the title, creating an imperial line that evolved into the [[Holy Roman Empire]].

Disputed, UN-designated non-self-governing territory in north-western Africa. Covering 272,000 sq km, it is the last African colonial state yet to achieve independence, and it is mostly desert flatland with an estimated 600,000 inhabitants. [[Spain]] colonized it as Spanish Sahara until 1975–1976, then attempted to transfer administration to [[Morocco]] and [[Mauritania]] despite an advisory opinion of the [[International Court of Justice]] that they had no sovereignty. A war followed, in which the pro-independence Polisario Front proclaimed the [[Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic]]. Mauritania withdrew its claims in 1979, and Morocco secured de facto control of most of the territory. A UN-sponsored ceasefire in 1991 was followed by a stalled referendum. Morocco maintains the Berm, a 2,700 km (1,700 mi) wall lined with land mines that splits the territory. The MINURSO mission was discontinued in November 2026 after the [[United Nations Security Council|Security Council]] failed to extend its mandate.

One of the four census regions of the United States, also called the American West. The U.S. Census Bureau defines it as the 13 westernmost states, from the [[Rocky Mountains]] to the Pacific Coast, including Alaska and Hawaii. Before around 1800 the Appalachian crest was the western frontier, and the term came to mean the lands west of the [[Mississippi River]]. The region covers nearly half the land area of the contiguous United States and contains major biomes, including arid plateaus and deserts, the [[Sierra Nevada]] and Pacific Northwest rainforests. The Mojave and Great Basin deserts lie entirely within it.

Transverse (side-blown) woodwind instrument, the common C concert flute and its family. Its relatives include the piccolo, alto flute and bass flute, and almost all are made of metal or wood, or both. The instrument is used in concert bands, military and marching bands, [[Orchestra|orchestras]], flute ensembles and occasionally [[Jazz|jazz]] combos and big bands, and it has a large repertory. Its precursors were keyless wooden transverse flutes similar to fifes, later modified with up to eight keys. The transverse flute reached Europe from Asia via the [[Byzantine Empire]], and in the Baroque period it was redesigned as the traverso with a conical bore. From 1832 the German flutist Theobald Boehm redesigned it with a metal body and a ring-key system. A player is called a "flautist" in British English and a "flutist" in American English.

Loosely related ideas and movements in Western society, also called the Western mystery tradition. Its currents are distinct from both orthodox Abrahamic religion and Enlightenment rationalism, and they have influenced philosophy, mysticism, science, pseudoscience, art, literature and music. The earliest traditions emerged in Late Antiquity, when [[Hermeticism]], [[Gnosticism]] and Neoplatonism developed in the Eastern Mediterranean. Renaissance thinkers combined pagan philosophy with [[Kabbalah]] and Christian ideas. The 17th century saw initiatory societies such as [[Rosicrucianism]] and [[Freemasonry]] emerge. In the 19th century, occultism included the Theosophical Society and the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. [[Modern paganism]], including [[Wicca]], developed within occultism. Esoteric ideas shaped the 1960s counterculture and the New Age phenomenon of the 1970s. Academic study of the field emerged only in the late 20th century.

Genre of fiction typically set on the American frontier, often called the Old West or Wild West. Most stories are set during westward expansion from the mid-19th century, around the California Gold Rush, through the closing of the frontier in 1890, though works may be set outside this period. The genre centers on cowboys, outlaws, sheriffs, gunslingers, settlers, soldiers and Native Americans, with themes of justice, freedom, rugged individualism, [[Manifest destiny|manifest destiny]] and conflict between civilization and wilderness. Stock plots often feature a crime, the pursuit of the wrongdoer, and revenge through a shootout or [[Duel|duel]]. Early Westerns often portrayed Native Americans as savage foes or through stereotypes, while later works were more sympathetic. The genre popularized country-Western music and Western wear. Its popularity peaked in Hollywood from the 1930s to the 1950s, with [[John Ford]]'s epic landscapes and [[John Wayne]]'s stoic heroes.

Most common of the 7–12 species of [[Honey bee|honey bees]] worldwide, *Apis mellifera*. The genus name *Apis* is Latin for "bee", and *mellifera* means "honey-bearing." Like all honey bees, it is eusocial, forming colonies with a single fertile queen, many sterile females called workers, and a small number of fertile males called drones. Colonies can house tens of thousands of bees, coordinated through [[Pheromone|pheromones]] and the waggle dance. One of the first domesticated insects, it remains the main species kept by beekeepers for honey and [[Pollination|pollination]]. Humans introduced European subspecies to North America in the early 1600s, and the species now occupies every continent except Antarctica. Varroa mites and colony collapse disorder threaten it, and the IUCN Red List rated it Data Deficient as of 2025.

Colonial and commercial domination of Asia by Western powers, from the 16th century. It originated in the 15th-century search for trade routes to India and Southeast Asia, prompted by Ottoman control of the [[Silk Road|Silk Road]]. The Portuguese reached India by way of the Cape of Good Hope in the 16th century, and the rival [[Dutch East India Company]] later eclipsed them, wresting Malacca, Ceylon and the Japan trade from them between 1640–60. After the Seven Years' War in 1763, the British eliminated French influence in India and made the [[East India Company]] the most important political force there. Before the [[Industrial Revolution]] of the 19th century, demand for porcelain, silk, spices and tea drove trade. The 1870s Long Depression provoked a scramble for new markets and the New Imperialism of direct colonial control. Formal colonial rule ended with the independence of Portuguese [[Macau]] in 1999.

Nations of Europe, the Americas and Australasia, also called the West and the Occident. Ancient Greece and Rome are regarded as the birthplaces of Western civilization. A geographical concept of the West took shape in the 4th century, when Constantine divided the Roman Empire between the Greek East and the Latin West. The [[East–West Schism]] of 1054 made the division definitive, and the [[Crusades]] failed to win eastern trade routes but instead "discovered" the Americas. After European colonization of the Americas, the idea of a Western world emerged as an heir to Latin Christendom; the earliest Oxford English Dictionary reference is from 1586. Australia and New Zealand are included in modern definitions, while Russia has been seen both as part of the West and in contrast to it. From the late 1960s, parts of the Western world became notable for diversity due to immigration.

[[Church of England|Anglican]] church in the City of Westminster, London, formally the Collegiate Church of Saint Peter at Westminster. Coronations of 40 English and British monarchs have taken place there since 1066, and 18 monarchs are buried there. More than 3,300 people are buried or commemorated in the abbey, including poets, scientists and the Unknown Warrior. Construction of the present church began in 1245 under Henry III, in the style of 13th-century French and English Gothic architecture. The monastery was dissolved in 1559, and [[Elizabeth I]] made the church a royal peculiar, directly accountable to the sovereign. The abbey has been a [[World Heritage Site]] since 1987.

Period of the year when most of a region's average annual rainfall falls, also called the rainy or monsoon season. Under the Köppen classification, a tropical wet-season month has average precipitation of 60 mm (2.4 in) or more. Wet seasons occur in warmer months in tropical savanna and monsoon climates, where rain falls mainly in the late afternoon and early evening as the [[Intertropical Convergence Zone]] moves. Vegetation grows and fresh water quality improves, but soil nutrients diminish, erosion increases, and [[Malaria|malaria]] and dengue rise where high temperatures coincide. Food shortages are common, since the previous dry season's crops have yet to mature. Crops planted in the wet season include [[Cassava]], [[Maize]], groundnut, millet, rice and yam. Tropical rainforests have no wet season, because their rainfall is spread evenly through the year.

Semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or saturated with water, permanently or seasonally. Flooding makes the soil oxygen-poor, and wetland plants have roots adapted to these waterlogged conditions. Wetlands form a transitional zone between water bodies and dry land and exist on every continent except Antarctica, with freshwater, brackish or saltwater. [[Marsh]]es are dominated by herbaceous plants such as reeds and cattails, [[Swamp]]s by trees and shrubs, and [[Mangrove]] forests by salt-tolerant woody plants. Wetlands are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems. They purify water, stabilize shorelines and control floods, and they store [[Carbon|carbon]] but can emit methane. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment of 2005 found them more threatened than any other ecosystem on Earth. Since 1971, an international treaty has worked to protect "wetlands of international importance."

Large marine mammal, an informal grouping of [[Cetacean|cetaceans]] apart from dolphins and porpoises. Whales are fully aquatic placental mammals whose closest living relatives are hippopotamuses, from which cetaceans diverged about 54 million years ago. Baleen whales (Mysticeti) filter [[Krill|krill]] and [[Plankton|plankton]] through baleen plates, while toothed whales (Odontoceti) have conical teeth for catching fish or [[Squid|squid]]. The [[Blue whale]] reaches 29.9 m (98 ft) and 190 tonnes, the largest known animal, while the dwarf sperm whale is 2.6 m (8.5 ft) long. Whales breathe through blowholes, are warm-blooded and insulated by blubber. Calves are typically born in spring and summer. Once relentlessly hunted, whales are now protected by international law, but the North Atlantic right whale nearly became extinct in the 20th century, dropping to a low of 450. Whale watching is now a major form of tourism.

Slow-moving, filter-feeding carpet shark, the largest living fish species. The only living species of the genus *Rhincodon* reaches 18.8 m (61.7 ft), the largest reliably recorded length, and is by far the largest living non-cetacean animal. It feeds on [[Plankton|plankton]], [[Krill|krill]], fish eggs and small schooling fish such as [[Sardine|sardines]], filtering over 6,000 liters of water an hour through its gill pads. It migrates across tropical oceans and gathers at coastal sites including Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia and off [[Gujarat]] and [[Kerala]] in India. It is docile toward humans, but the IUCN Red List lists it as Endangered after a population decline of more than 50% over the last 75 years, caused by targeted fishing, bycatch and ship collisions. Despite its name, it is a fish, not a mammal, and is not closely related to [[Whale|whales]].

Hunting of whales for meat, blubber and other products. Blubber could be rendered into oil that was important in the [[Industrial Revolution]]. The earliest well-documented industry dates to 1026 in the Basque coastal regions of Spain and France, and it spread through the North Atlantic. Subsistence whaling of small cetaceans by the [[Inuit]] and other peoples dates to at least 3000 BC, and a 2026 study dates whaling of baleen whales to at least 5,000 years ago in southern Brazil. Commercial fleets grew from the 17th century, and factory ships and explosive harpoons came in the first half of the 20th century; by the late 1930s more than 50,000 whales were killed annually. In 1982 the International Whaling Commission decided on a five-year pause on commercial whaling from 1986, which has since been extended indefinitely. [[Iceland]], [[Japan]] and [[Norway]] still hunt commercially, and whale watching has become a significant industry in many parts of the world.

American instant messaging and Voice over IP app owned by Meta Platforms. Launched in May 2009 by Brian Acton and Jan Koum, former [[Yahoo]] employees, it lets users send text, voice and video messages, make calls and share images, documents and locations. Registration requires a cellular mobile telephone number. [[Facebook]] acquired WhatsApp in February 2014 for approximately US$19.3 billion. As of May 2025 it had 3 billion monthly active users, making it the most popular messenger app. WhatsApp Business, a standalone app, was released in January 2018.

Simple machine: a [[Wheel|wheel]] fixed coaxially to a smaller [[Axle|axle]]. The two parts rotate together and transfer force from one to the other, so the device can be viewed as a version of the [[Lever|lever]], with the drive force applied to the rim and the load on the axle, which is supported in a [[Bearing (mechanical)|bearing]] as fulcrum. Freely spinning [[Potter's wheel|potter's wheels]] were developed in [[Mesopotamia]] by 4200–4000 BC, and the oldest surviving example, from [[Ur]], dates to about 3100 BC. Wheeled vehicles appeared in the late 4th millennium BC. A wooden wheel and axle from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia is between 5,100 and 5,350 years old, by radiocarbon dating. [[Hero of Alexandria]] identified the wheel and axle as one of the simple machines used to lift weights, and Renaissance scientists later counted it among six simple machines.

Small hand-propelled vehicle, usually with a single [[Wheel|wheel]], guided by two handles at the rear. It spreads a load between the wheel and the operator, making it a second-class [[Lever|lever]] that carries heavier loads than a person could alone. Typical capacity is about 100 liters (3.53 cubic feet), and it is common in [[Construction|construction]] and [[Gardening|gardening]]. Two-wheeled types are more stable on level ground, while one-wheel types maneuver better in small spaces and on planks. The earliest archaeological evidence is a one-wheel cart in [[Han dynasty|Han dynasty]] tomb murals and reliefs, including a Chengdu, Sichuan mural dated to 118 AD of a man pushing one. The [[Three Kingdoms]] text Sanguozhi credits [[Zhuge Liang]] with a wooden ox used to transport military supplies in 231 AD. Chinese wheelbarrows with large central wheels were common, and the wheelbarrow did not reach Europe until the [[Middle Ages]].
